title: How Worker Co-ops Works
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explain worker cooperatives (co-ops), tracing their roots from Robert Owen's Owenism and New Harmony, Indiana, through the Rochdale Pioneers in England, Black cooperatives in the post-Civil War United States, and the Knights of Labor. They cover the Rochdale Principles, how co-op membership and governance work, support organizations, the Mondragon Corporation in Spain, the Indian labor cooperative in Kerala, Italy's and Argentina's support for worker buyouts, Mexican fishing co-ops, and US examples including Cooperative Home Care Associates, Maximum Fun, Island Employee Cooperative in Maine, employee stock ownership plans, Publix, and ACE Hardware. They close with pros and cons and a listener mail segment about Ponty City tower in Johannesburg.

entities.name: Colored Farmers National Alliance and Cooperative Society

segments.title: Intro: co-ops versus the capitalist model
segments.summary: Hosts introduce worker cooperatives, note the hyphenated spelling, and contrast the familiar US co-op grocery Sevenanda with the idea that workers own and profit from their business.

segments.title: Robert Owen and Owenism
segments.summary: Robert Owen, a Welsh mill owner, tried a utopian community at New Harmony, Indiana, in 1825, which did not last long; his ideas inspired co-op movements in the US and UK.

segments.title: Socialism and the way the US discusses it
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how early co-op ideas were socialist in nature and how the term socialism is treated in the United States.

segments.title: Rochdale Pioneers and the first co-op store
segments.summary: Weavers in Rochdale, England, formed the Rochdale Friendly Cooperative Society, a retail store where members shared profits; this is described as the basis of co-ops.

segments.title: Second Rochdale society and the Cooperative Group
segments.summary: The Rochdale society failed after a couple of years, was reformed around 1844 as the Society of Equitable Pioneers with a membership fee and plans for housing and farming, and its store model became the basis of later co-ops; it grew into the UK Cooperative Group.

segments.title: Large co-op groups
segments.summary: Hosts note that the largest co-ops are often groups of co-ops, with examples in Spain and India to come.

segments.title: Black cooperatives after the Civil War
segments.summary: Black workers in Baltimore formed the Colored Calkers Trade Union Society, led by Isaac Myers, which bought a shipyard and railways. The hosts also briefly discuss the origin of the contractor saying about shoddy work.

segments.title: Colored Farmers National Alliance and labor republicanism
segments.summary: After the Civil War, black farmers excluded from the Southern Farmers Alliance formed the Colored Farmers National Alliance and Cooperative Society, which had a million or more members by 1891. The hosts also introduce labor republicanism, the idea that control over one's own work provides freedom.

segments.title: Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor
segments.summary: The Knights of Labor, a large union that nearly reached a million members by the 1880s, promoted worker cooperatives, but the more business-friendly American Federation of Labor became larger. The International Cooperative Alliance formed in 1895.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: How co-ops are run: Rochdale Principles and governance
segments.summary: The hosts cover the Rochdale Principles adopted by the ICA in 1995: voluntary open membership, one member one vote (versus share-based voting), democratic control of capital, autonomy, member education, cooperation among co-ops, and community service. They also discuss probationary periods, buy-in, and how larger co-ops elect boards.

segments.title: Support organizations for converting to co-ops
segments.summary: Northwest Cooperative Development Center and Cooperative Fund of the Northeast are named as resources for converting an existing business into a co-op or starting one from scratch.

segments.title: Mondragon Corporation in Spain
segments.summary: Mondragon, a collective of around 95 co-ops in the Basque region of Spain, was founded by priest José María Arizmendiarrieta; it began in 1956 with five workers making kerosene heaters and now employs about 80,000. Its members vote on strategy and pay, it has a probationary period, and its top pay is capped at six times the lowest salary, versus about 350 to one at a typical US corporation.

segments.title: Co-ops during economic downturns
segments.summary: Co-ops tend to share pain through pay cuts instead of layoffs, in contrast to capitalist firms.

segments.title: India's labor contract cooperative
segments.summary: The Lungal Labor Contract Cooperative Society in Kerala, India, founded in 1925 under British rule by sixteen lower-caste workers repairing roads, now has about 18,000 employees. Hosts note Nehru encouraged worker and farmer co-ops.

segments.title: Italy, Argentina, and Mexico co-op examples
segments.summary: Italy supports co-ops with financial incentives and helps employees buy failing companies. Argentina's National Movement of Recovered Companies, in the early 2000s, saw laid-off workers take over about 400 factories. Mexico has strong fishing co-ops that self-police sustainability.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Co-ops in the United States
segments.summary: Only about 7,000 to 10,000 Americans work in co-ops. The largest is Cooperative Home Care Associates in the Bronx, founded in 1985 by twelve home health aides, with about 2,000 workers; workers can buy in for about $1,000 and job satisfaction is reported as higher.

segments.title: Maximum Fun becomes a worker co-op
segments.summary: Jesse Thorn, sole owner of podcast company Maximum Fun, transitioned it to a worker-owned co-op about three years ago after deciding to step back.

segments.title: Island Employee Cooperative in Maine
segments.summary: Three Maine island stores (the Galley, VNS Variety, and Burnt Cove Market) were bought by workers when owners could not find buyers, forming the Island Employee Cooperative with about 70 members, headquartered in Stonington, Maine. Hosts joke about Maine islands and Murder, She Wrote.

segments.title: ESOPs, Publix, and ACE Hardware
segments.summary: Employee stock ownership plans are discussed as related but distinct from co-ops, since workers usually don't get votes. Publix is described as the largest employee-owned company in the US, with employees owning about 80 percent. ACE Hardware is a cooperative of independent retailers, and the hosts say returns between stores may not be accepted for online purchases.

segments.title: Pros and cons of co-ops
segments.summary: Pros include a narrow pay gap, low layoff rates, and worker self-policing that keeps productivity up; cons include slower decision-making in a crisis. Co-ops are said to last longer than many startups and workers report greater job satisfaction. Hosts also mention Subvert (alternative to Bandcamp) and Fair (rideshare co-op alternative to Uber and Lyft).

segments.title: Listener mail: Ponty City tower
segments.summary: Listener Bobby writes about Ponty City tower in Johannesburg, completed in 1975 as a luxury development that decayed into what is called the world's first vertical slum; it has appeared in sci-fi films.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Bobby and invite listener emails; show credits follow.
